Kohberger previously agreed to four consecutive life sentences without parole roughly a year ago to avoid capital punishment, formally affirming under oath before Judge Steven Hippler that he was acting voluntarily and entering the plea because he was guilty.

Under Idaho Rule 33, post-sentencing plea withdrawals require proof of a "manifest injustice," forcing the defense to provide substantial, concrete evidence of coercion, fraud, or ineffective counsel to vacate the conviction.

Judge Steven Hippler oversaw the change-of-plea hearing where Kohberger previously affirmed under oath that he understood the agreement and was acting voluntarily, creating a credibility gap his defense must overcome.

With more than 67,000 cases pending in the federal MDL, Levin Papantonio attorneys secured a $20 million Florida jury verdict for Alberto Casaretto's family in October 2025, demonstrating the litigation's scope.

Erik Haas, Johnson & Johnson's litigation head, said the agreement lets the company "put this matter behind it," while lawyers representing the plaintiffs welcomed the settlement as resolution to a decade-long court battle.

The Supreme Court determined that patent owners cannot circumvent FRAND obligations by joining a licensing pool like Avanci. Tesla's separate claim to revoke three InterDigital patents is also allowed to proceed.

Following the decision, the case returns to the High Court for further proceedings. Laurie Fitzgerald, president of Avanci Vehicle, said, "We respectfully disagree with today's decision and continue to believe Tesla's claims are without merit."

Technology lobbying group CCIA and the Motion Picture Association supported Tesla during the appeal, intervening to emphasize broader implications for how patent holders engage with licensing platforms in the United Kingdom.
title: Tesla wins bid to revive UK lawsuit for 5G patents licence

summary: Tomorrow and Thursday, The Southern Delta Aquariids meteor shower will peak in Singapore, with the Science Centre Observatory confirming the phenomenon will appear on July 29 and 30.

During the peak, Earth passes through dust and debris left by Comet Machholz Complex, with particles burning up in the atmosphere to create the bright streaks known as 'shooting stars.' The shower draws its name from the constellation Aquarius.

Ideal viewing occurs between 2am and 5.30am in dark areas away from city lights, with suitable locations including East Coast Park, Changi Beach Park, West Coast Park, Marina Barrage, and the Southern Ridges.

While no special equipment is needed, viewers should allow 20 minutes to 30 minutes for eyes to adjust to darkness. However, the Moon may obscure some meteors as the peak coincides with the full moon on July 29.

Observers can see up to 25 meteors an hour under ideal conditions, though actual numbers are usually lower due to light pollution. The next major meteor shower visible from Singapore is the Perseid, peaking around Aug 12 to 13.
title: Double meteor showers peak this week, but the moon may steal the show

A Google user posted the "Worst Aquarium Ever" review in 2020, mocking the institution's focus on whaling history rather than live marine exhibits. The New Bedford, Massachusetts museum houses whale skeletons and artifacts, not live aquatic animals.

Following a CBS Evening News segment on Wednesday night, customers placed 738 online orders by Thursday afternoon. Weekly orders surged 250% compared to the prior week, driven by the museum's self-deprecating marketing strategy.

Visitor Experience Manager Emily Roznoy and Chief Engagement Officer Annelise Conway are managing the surge by coordinating with local printer Cape Cod Textiles. The museum, lacking a dedicated shipping department, has enlisted staff to pack orders.

The hospital committed $30 million to create the Institute for Safe Patient Care and Patient Empowerment, adding to over $1 billion in civil settlements previously agreed to pay victims.
Under the new resolution, WCM must expand chaperone requirements, centralize complaint reporting, and conduct periodic reviews until 2031, while acknowledging previous policies were inadequate.

U.S. Attorney Jay Clayton said the agreement sends a "strong, clear message to all healthcare institutions," as the system faces scrutiny alongside recent abuse convictions for doctors Robert Hadden and Zhi Allen Cheng.

Embracing the term 'genocide' to describe Israel's war in Gaza, Jackson pledged to reject 'dark money' from corporate PACs and AIPAC, positioning himself as a progressive alternative to Senator Susan Collins.

Day triggered a massive emergency services response when he climbed Elizabeth Tower on March 8, 2025, and occupied the landmark barefoot for 17 hours while livestreaming and chanting 'Free Palestine'.
The 17-hour incident cost taxpayers at least £92,000, including £67,000 from more than 2,500 cancelled Parliament tours and an estimated £25,000 in lost TfL bus fares during road closures.
Judge Baumgartner ordered Day to attend up to 20 rehabilitation days and remain under electronic monitoring for four months as conditions of the suspended sentence.
Baumgartner noted Day showed 'little insight into your offending or any real remorse,' though he acknowledged failing eyesight as strong personal mitigation for the well-planned protest.
title: Pro-Palestine protester dodges jail after climbing Big Ben tower

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames AIPAC as “dropping” Democrats and even stripping “plaudits,” centering donor punishment and intra-party signaling; right-leaning coverage casts the same move as “freezes out” or retaliation against Democrats who “voted against aid to Israel,” treating the vote as a rebuke of an ally.
Centered coverage stays more procedural, noting the fundraising freeze and the $3.3 billion aid cut.
The sharpest dividing line is whether the vote is a policy disagreement or an anti-Israel act.
Both sides agree AIPAC selectively removed donation options, but the ideological split turns on loyalty, pressure, and the meaning of support for Israel.
summary: On Friday, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee suspended fundraising for more than two dozen House Democrats who backed an amendment to slash $3.3 billion in military aid to Israel, removing donation links from its online portal.
Rep. Thomas Massie introduced the measure to the fiscal 2027 State Department funding bill, which was defeated Wednesday by a 104-314-10 vote despite support from more than 100 Democrats.

Affected members include House Minority Whip Katherine Clark and former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, who received roughly $1.4 million and more than $19,000 respectively in AIPAC-related contributions according to Federal Election Commission records.

Defending his vote on Thursday, Rep. Jake Auchincloss stated Congress "must act where the executives have failed," as the suspension reflects AIPAC's consistent strategy of linking campaign support to voting records, previously applied to 15 Republican lawmakers in 2024.

Legislative records show 104 Democrats voted to cut aid this week, reflecting a broader realignment within the Democratic Party regarding unconditional support for Israel amid the humanitarian crisis in Gaza.
title: AIPAC halts fundraising for endorsed House Democrats who opposed Israel aid

bias: Left-Leaning coverage turns the Al-Aqsa episode into a sweeping moral indictment, using terms like “settler terrorism,” “genocide,” and “occupied territories” to portray Israeli actions as illegal and deeply provocative, while listing the eight Arab-Islamic states to underscore diplomatic breadth.

Right-Leaning coverage keeps the condemnation but shifts blame onto “extremist Israeli ministers,” “mass settlers’ incursions,” and Israeli forces’ protection, stressing state complicity rather than legal accusations.
A key dividing line is whether the incident is framed as a broader rights crisis or a minister-led security breach.
Both sides agree on escalation and condemnation, reflecting a shared focus on sovereignty, sacred space, and regional conflict.
summary: On Friday, the foreign ministers of eight Arab-Islamic states condemned Israeli escalation at Al-Aqsa Mosque, citing mass settler incursions into the holy place under the protection of Israeli forces.

Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir led settlers into the mosque compound on Thursday, prompting the joint condemnation from Jordan, the UAE, Indonesia, Pakistan, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and Egypt.

The ministers stressed that the entire 144-dunum Al-Aqsa Mosque compound is an exclusive Muslim place of worship, with the Jerusalem Waqf and Al-Aqsa Mosque Affairs Department as the sole legal authority administering the site.

These actions violate international law and the historical status quo in occupied East Jerusalem, the ministers stated, while urging the international community to take decisive action against ongoing violations affecting Islamic and Christian holy sites.

Repeated incursions and inflammatory rhetoric risk increasing regional tensions while obstructing efforts to advance a just and lasting peace on the basis of the two-state solution, as the FMs called for Israel to lift access restrictions to the Old City.
title: Arab states condemn Israel's Quds escalation

bias: Left-Leaning coverage turns back-to-school inflation into a political indictment, using phrases like “severe sticker shock,” “crushed,” and “Trump’s policies” to frame higher prices as a direct consequence of conservative leadership and even an election liability, while right-leaning coverage is de-emphasized here, leaving the main contrast with the center: a more restrained, report-style emphasis on prices “surged” and costs running more than double inflation.

The dividing line is blame—left outlets spotlight partisan causation and emotional hardship, while the less ideological framing treats the same 8% increase and 27% lunch-box jump as a consumer-price trend.
Both sides agree families are paying more, but they diverge on whether that signals policy failure or simply rising costs.
summary: A joint analysis from the Groundwork Collaborative and The Century Foundation released Monday reveals a typical basket of school supplies costs nearly 8% more than last year, with school lunch items surging 11%.
Driving these increases are tariffs on foreign imports and the ongoing war in Iran, which has spiked fuel and shipping costs that filter through to consumer goods, according to the report.

Lunch boxes have climbed nearly 27%, while notebooks and index cards have also soared; Victoria Albano of Duluth, Georgia, said she spent about $230 at Target for her daughter's school supplies despite cost pressures.

Financial stress intensifies as 1.5 million children have lost Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits, while about half of parents now expect to take on debt to cover back-to-school shopping this year.

As midterm elections approach, ParentsTogether executive director Ailen Arreaza noted families are increasingly focused on systemic economic pressures; about 70 percent of parents cite experiencing financial strain with little relief in sight.
title: Analysis Finds Back-to-School Supply and Lunch Costs Have Increased Since 2025

summary: On Sunday, Last Week Tonight host John Oliver exposed ethical concerns regarding President Donald Trump 's family cryptocurrency businesses, which have become their dominant financial interest.
Trump's personal income surged to more than $2.2 billion in his first year back in office, mostly from family crypto ventures that typically spike then crash after insiders sell at peaks.

Chinese billionaire Justin Sun invested $75 million in World Liberty Financial while an Emirati official nicknamed The Spy Sheikh contributed $500 million, raising questions about foreign influence and access.

The administration is pushing the CLARITY Act to shift crypto regulation from the SEC to the short-staffed Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which critics argue lacks investor protection mandates.

Trump, who previously called Bitcoin a 'scam' and 'a disaster waiting to happen,' now brands himself the 'first crypto president,' though Oliver warns that lacking proper guardrails leaves the system vulnerable to exploitation.
title: John Oliver Criticizes Trump's Cryptocurrency Ventures, Including World Liberty Financial, on 'Last Week Tonight'

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames Trump’s WHCD remarks as an “attack” or “mockery,” spotlighting Mulvaney’s defiant comeback and even casting the joke as a kind of public backlash against a transgender figure.

Right-Leaning coverage, by contrast, leans into culture-war shorthand—words like “roast,” “ridiculed,” and “trans activist”—to present the episode as a pointed jab at a controversial Bud Light-linked symbol and to emphasize Trump’s “humorous and defiant” posture.
The main fault line is whether the moment signals harm or ridicule versus comedic political theater.
Both sides agree Trump singled out Mulvaney and Kaitlan Collins, but they diverge on whether that exchange reveals hostility or spectacle.
summary: Influencer Dylan Mulvaney responded on Sunday to President Donald Trump 's remarks at the White House Correspondents' Dinner, calling his comparison to CNN anchor Kaitlan Collins a "compliment."
President Trump used the dinner to mock Mulvaney's 2023 Bud Light partnership while simultaneously insulting Collins for not smiling, a recurring grievance he has previously voiced.

Trump claimed the 2023 partnership cost Bud Light $35 billion in market capitalization; following the event, the president posted an AI-generated image superimposing Collins' face onto Mulvaney's commercial.
Mulvaney stated she was "incredibly honored" to be compared to Collins and urged support for trans and nonbinary people, framing the mockery as evidence of her own power.

These remarks continue Trump's pattern of hostility toward Collins, whom he frequently labels "fake news." The use of AI-generated media to intensify conflict reflects a broader shift in how public figures leverage technology.
title: Dylan Mulvaney responds to Trump: ‘I am microchipped into their minds’

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames Jay Clayton’s move toward confirmation as a procedural step toward a “permanent director,” stressing the need for stability before the midterms, while right-leaning coverage turns the same vote into a national-security story, spotlighting “Section 702,” “anti-terror,” and a program in “limbo.” The right also uses sharper, more partisan shorthand like “top spy,” “turbulent,” and “curveballs,” making the process feel urgent and combative; the left stays more restrained and institutional.
The key dividing line is whether the nomination is mainly about staffing or restoring spy powers.
Both agree on the 51-43 vote and looming final vote, but they connect it to different ideological priorities.
summary: On Monday, the Senate voted 51-43 to advance President Donald Trump 's nominee, Attorney Jay Clayton, for Director of National Intelligence through a procedural cloture motion, clearing the path for a final confirmation vote later this week.

The Senate Intelligence Committee recommended Clayton in a narrow 9-8 vote last week after President Trump postponed his hearing mid-June, forcing Republicans to advance the nomination to avoid prolonged interim leadership.

During his July 15 hearing, Clayton faced criticism for refusing to say President Joe Biden won the 2020 election and for issuing subpoenas to New York Times journalists investigating Trump administration security concerns.

Virginia Sen. Mark Warner and other Democrats remain opposed to Clayton but acknowledged being "between a rock and a hard place" with interim director Federal Housing Finance Agency Director Bill Pulte, a Trump loyalist lacking national security experience.

Established after the September 11, 2001, attacks, the DNI role requires deep expertise to oversee 18 intelligence agencies, with Clayton expected to be confirmed along party lines before midterm elections approach.
title: US Senate votes to advance Trump nominee Clayton to be top US spy

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the ruling as a check on state overreach, stressing “preempted by federal law” and broader litigation actors like the Justice Department and CFTC, while right-leaning coverage strips the story to a market-friendly judicial “blocks” a state “ban,” with little legal context.

The sharpest divide is over how Minnesota ’s law is portrayed: the left highlights federal-state conflict and gambling-like concerns, whereas the right foregrounds regulatory restraint and treats the ban as excessive.

Center coverage sits between them, adding “first-in-nation,” “preliminary injunction,” and “early legal victory.” All sides agree the judge halted enforcement, but they diverge on whether that is protection from overreach or defeat for regulation.
summary: On Monday, a federal judge granted a preliminary injunction blocking Minnesota from enforcing its ban on prediction markets , pausing the law until a final decision on the merits is reached.

Gov. Walz signed the ban in May, prompting lawsuits from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, Kalshi, and Polymarket, who argue federal law preempts state authority and cite First Amendment violations.

Former Democratic Senator Christopher Dodd argued lawmakers never intended to make the CFTC a gambling regulator, while former CFTC Chairman Timothy Massad claimed the agency "has lost its way" regarding its mission.

Attorney General Keith Ellison responded that Minnesota "respectfully disagree" with the ruling, calling prediction markets "predatory gambling" and confirming the state will continue to defend its law.

Native American tribes, casinos, and local authorities in 20 states warn that prediction markets constitute illegal gambling, while President Donald Trump and his administration have generally embraced the industry, arguing federal law protects registered markets.
title: Judge blocks Minnesota's first-in-nation prediction markets ban

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the case as a civil-liberties dispute, stressing the commission as “so-called” and “overwhelmingly conservative Christian,” with plaintiffs’ claims of a “biased body” and “unlawful” composition; right-leaning coverage flips the emphasis to vindication, using sharper celebratory or dismissive terms like “clean victory,” “tosses,” and “signature faith-based” to portray the lawsuit as an overreach against a legitimate “religious liberty” panel.
The key dividing line is whether the ruling signals exclusion and imbalance or legal confirmation and mission defense, though both sides note the judge’s dismissal.
Broader divides surface in how each side treats faith, authority, and the Trump administration ’s role.
summary: On Monday, U.S. District Judge John Cronan dismissed a lawsuit challenging President Donald Trump 's Religious Liberty Commission, ruling the advisory panel does not violate federal requirements that such committees be "fairly balanced."

The lawsuit, filed in February by the Interfaith Alliance, Muslim, and Hindu groups, argued the Religious Liberty Commission violated rules by excluding non-Judeo-Christian faith traditions and consisted almost entirely of conservative Christians with one Orthodox Jewish rabbi.

Cronan wrote that "The RLC must only be fairly balanced—not perfectly balanced," rejecting claims that Trump was required to appoint representatives from every faith tradition or adopt a quota system.

Organizations including Democracy Forward and Americans United for Separation of Church and State stated their litigation "helped uncover the information the Trump-Vance administration attempted to hide from the public about this biased and unlawful body."

Trump established the Religious Liberty Commission last year under Texas Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick and Urban Development Secretary Ben Carson, and critics said its June draft report challenged the separation of church and state while failing to address anti-Muslim attacks.
title: Federal judge dismisses a lawsuit over makeup of Trump's Religious Liberty Commission
